extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and political philosophy; scholars interested in ethics, punishment theory, and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Close-philosophical exposition of the nature and justification of punishment, the distinction between temporal and eternal justice, and the meanings of 'good' and 'bad', with reference to law, state, and metaphysical grounds. Aimed at explaining normative criteria for justice and virtue within a metaphysical framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment grounded in positive law (social contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punish is based upon the positive law alone, which before the offence has determined a punishment for it, the threat of which, as a counter-motive, is intended to outweigh all possible motives for the offence. This positive law ... is to be regarded as sanctioned and recognised by all the members of the state. It is thus based upon a common contract which the members of the state are in duty bound to fulfil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must be enacted by law accepted within the state and understood as part of the mutual contract of citizens (they must both inflict and endure the punishment). The legitimacy of punishment rests on this contractual/legal basis rather than on individual moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterrence (future-oriented end) as the immediate end of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate end of punishment is the fulfilment of the law as a contract. But the one end of the law is deterrence from the infringement of the rights of others ... the law and the fulfilment of it, the punishment, are essentially directed to the future, not to the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment is justified instrumentally to prevent future wrongdoing by creating counter-motives. Legal language (e.g., historic indictment phrasing) and executive restraint (e.g., cautioning mercy because it may encourage repetition) illustrate this forward-looking justification. Punishment must announce itself as inevitable in future cases to secure deterrent effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice of punishment requires enactment and generalizability (not arbitrary vengeance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An end for the future distinguishes punishment from revenge, and punishment only has this end when it is inflicted in fulfilment of a law. It thus announces itself as inevitable in every future case, and thus the law obtains the power to deter, in which its end really consists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For punishment to be morally and politically just, it must not be a private, selective act but a legal, general rule applied with the intention of future prevention. Arbitrary or private requital lacks this justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of mere requital/retributivism (jus talionis criticized)
rubrics_metrics.description: All requital of wrong by the infliction of pain, without any aim for the future, is revenge, and can have no other end than consolation for the suffering one has borne ... The jus talionis set up as the absolute, final principle of the right of punishment, is meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment justified solely as expiation or neutralisation of past wrongdoing (requital for its own sake) is morally indefensible—described as wickedness and cruelty. The text argues against setting oneself up as a private moral judge imposing penance.

rubrics_metrics.name: State's duty to protect society by interdiction and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Man has the right to care for the safety of society; and this can only be done by interdicting all actions which are denoted by the word 'criminal,' in order to prevent them by means of counter-motives, which are the threatened punishments. And this threat can only be made effective by carrying it out when a case occurs in spite of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state is justified in imposing prohibitions and enforcing punishments to secure collective safety; enforcement (carrying out threatened punishments) is necessary to maintain deterrent credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment's legitimacy vs Kantian 'never treat as mere means' objection
rubrics_metrics.description: A Kantian would inevitably reply that ... the punished criminal would be used 'merely as a means.' ... The murderer who has been condemned to the punishment of death according to law must now, at any rate, and with complete right, be used as a mere means. For public security ... is disturbed by him; indeed it is abolished if the law is not carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text responds to the Kantian objection by arguing that using a criminal instrumentally to re-establish public security is justified by the social contract: the criminal has forfeited certain claims by violating the mutual pledge that underwrites security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between temporal justice (state) and eternal justice (world/thing-in-itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal justice, which has its seat in the state, is requiting and punishing, and have seen that this only becomes justice through a reference to the future. But it is quite otherwise with eternal justice ... which rules not the state but the world, is not dependent upon human institutions, is not subject to chance and deception, is not uncertain, wavering, and erring, but infallible, fixed, and sure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal (legal) justice operates by delay and generalizable punishment; eternal justice is metaphysical, inseparably binding punishment and offence, and cannot be satisfied by temporal requital. Understanding the difference matters for moral theory and religious/mythical accounts of retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternal justice not expressible as temporal requital
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of requital implies that of time; therefore eternal justice cannot be requital. Thus it cannot, like temporal justice, admit of respite and delay, and require time in order to triumph, equalising the evil deed by the evil consequences only by means of time. The punishment must here be so bound up with the offence that both are one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one appeals to eternal justice, one must conceive of punishment and offence as immediately and inseparably connected (a metaphysical binding), not as separated events bridged by time or legal processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth (transmigration, karma) as a practical ethical teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The myth of the transmigration of souls ... teaches that all sufferings which in life one inflicts upon other beings must be expiated in a subsequent life in this world, through precisely the same sufferings ... as a reward ... it promises re-birth in better, nobler forms ... or, as the Buddhists ... 'Thou shalt attain to Nirvâna.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious or mythical doctrines can serve as effective, perception-grounded moral pedagogy: myths translate metaphysical truths into behavioural incentives and sanctions comprehensible within the principium individuationis (exoteric teaching). They function as postulates of practical reason when direct philosophical knowledge is inaccessible to the masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private vengeance that aims at future deterrence can resemble punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: We sometimes see a man ... stakes his own life in order to take vengeance ... If, now, we consider the spirit of that desire for retribution carefully, we find that it is very different from common revenge ... For in it there really lies the intention of an effect upon the future through the example ... without any selfish aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When individuals enact vengeance intending a general deterrent example (not mere consolation), such acts resemble punishment in aim, though they lack legal sanction and may be condemned by the state. This nuance separates pure revenge from morally 'punishing' sacrifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good defined as conformity to the will's effort (relative, not absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: This concept is essentially relative, and signifies the conformity of an object to any definite effort of the will. Accordingly everything that corresponds to the will in any of its expressions and fulfils its end is thought through the concept 'good' ... The conception of the good divides itself into two sub-species—that of the direct and present satisfaction ... and that of its indirect satisfaction which has reference to the future, i.e., the agreeable and the useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'good' only relatively: what furthers a will's particular aim is 'good' (good food, good roads, good people insofar as they further ends). Distinguish immediate agreeable satisfaction and instrumental usefulness; avoid treating 'good' as an unanalyzed absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute good (summum bonum) impossible except via denial of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute good is, therefore, a contradiction in terms; highest good, summum bonum, really signifies ... a final satisfaction of the will, after which no new desire could arise ... such a consummation is not even thinkable ... we may ... call the complete self-effacement and denial of the will, the true absence of will ... the absolute good, the summum bonum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within this metaphysical-ethical system, lasting ultimate good cannot be achieved by fulfilling will-driven desires; only the radical negation or renunciation of the will (akin to Buddhist nirvana) yields permanent cessation of striving and thus the only plausible notion of 'absolute good.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad (evil) as non-conformity to the will and as denial of others' will (egoism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the conception 'bad' ... denotes everything that does not correspond to any effort of the will. If a man is always disposed to do wrong whenever the opportunity presents itself ... we call him bad. According to our doctrine of wrong, this means that such a man does not merely assert the will to live as it appears in his own body, but in this assertion goes so far that he denies the will which appears in other individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral badness arises from extreme egoism that seeks to appropriate or destroy others' powers in service of one's own will. The ethical inquiry must account both for objective effects on others and the agent's inner disposition; 'bad' is thus evaluated relative to the thwarting of other wills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of eternal justice requires transcending individuation (principium individuationis)
rubrics_metrics.description: That man only will grasp and comprehend eternal justice who raises himself above the knowledge that proceeds under the guidance of the principle of sufficient reason, bound to the particular thing, and recognises the Ideas, sees through the principium individuationis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True insight into eternal justice and the deepest ethical truths demands a metaphysical or contemplative transcendence of ordinary individuated perspective; such knowledge is rare and not required for the practice of virtue but explains why myths and religious systems persist as accessible substitutes.
